names.derivation: In Gītā we read: "One who chants my name Om and leaves his body at the time of death thus remembering Me, he shall go to the Supreme State" In Sanskrit, kṣara means the "perishable" and Akshara means the "imperishable." The world of plurality, the "perishable" is no doubt nothing other than the All — Perfect, the Immutable Truth, but due to the imperfections of the instruments-of-perception—body, mind and intellect—the perceiving ego can experience only this world constituted of a plurality—sense objects, emotions and thoughts—The ego peeping through the vehicles can never experience the One co-ordinating Reality, the Divine.
names.grammar: The name is used as a nominative singular expression; its head is spaṣṭākṣara.

names.derivation: Vāsu means "One who dwells in the physical equipments of all living creatures as its indweller (jīva-जीव); Deva means "One who revels or One who illumines". Thus, Vaasudevah means "One who lives in the physical equipment as though conditioned by them, and yet, who is the Vital Consciousness in the light of which every experience is illumined. Also, directly, it can be taken to mean, One who is born as the Son of Śrī Vasudeva in the Jail of Kamsa, the Blue — Boy of Brindaavana. He is called Vāsu as He veils Himself with His own Masyaa; Deva means "He who sports, wishes to conquer, conducts, shines, creates and moves".

According to Mahābhārata, "We call Him as Daamodara as He is known by means of Dama." Brahmapurana re-capitulates the incident in the early childhood of the Lord when He was tied with a cord (daama) round His waste (udara). names.derivation: When considered as one word it means: "One who creates many omniscient men of wisdom." One who encourages the spread of knowledge and thus turns out many men of wisdom and clearer understanding of life and the world. Or taken as two words its interpretation can mean: "One who is Omniscient and Vyasa." This would mean, "The Lord who has expressed Himself as Śrī Veda Vyasa." Vyasa is the poet-philosopher who codified, compiled and edited the Vedas and published them in four volumes—Rig Veda, with its 21 branches; Yajur Veda, with its 101 branches: Sāma Veda, with its 1000 branches and the Atharvana Veda, with its 9 branches (or Saakhaas).

names.derivation: Or “One Who is Vāsu and Deva.” “Vāsu” means "One who dwells in all creatures as their ego-centric individuality (jīva-roopa)." 'Deva' means "One Who revels." Therefore, this name for Lord Kṛṣṇa has the appropriate meaning: "One Who revels in every living creature as the jīva-entity in each." ‘‘ईश्वरः सर्वभूतानां हृद्देशेऽर्जुन तिष्ठति । भ्रामयन्सर्वभतानि यन्त्रारूढानि मायया ॥" (Īśvaraḥ sarvabhootaanaam hriddese Arjuna tisthati: Bhraamayan sarvabhootaani yantraaroodhaani maayayaa.) "The Lord dwells in the hearts of all beings, O Arjuna, causing all beings, by His illusive power, to revolve as if mounted on a machine.' -Gītā Ch.
